I'll start.

Keep your bike inside your home near the door. It's faster to get on it and ride, it's easier to develop a relationship with the bike when you're able to see it all the time, and you'll find that you ride it a lot more.

Keep your bike clean. Cleaning your bike can be as quick as a few minutes if you practice at it and do it regularly. Having a clean bike will make it work better and last longer. To the average person, even a cheap but clean and well maintained bike will look superior to a more expensive bike if the more expensive bike is dirty.* A clean bike is also welcome in a surprising amount of places that a dirty bike would be instantly turned away from.

Always have a backup. Unforeseen things can happen. Maybe your bike gets stolen, or maybe it gets a mechanical issue you can't fix quickly. If you don't have a spare bike that's ready to ride, you're just fucked. If you're trying to use a bike as a main source of transportation, you're double fucked.

Try to learn how to fix and adjust things by yourself. You'd be surprised how many things you can fix and tune on a bike with nothing more than your portable multi-tool, and you'll save yourself incalculable amounts of time and money in the long run.

Learn your bike fit. Your bike frame should be the correct size for your body, and you should have the correct saddle height and position as well as handlebar distance and handlebar height. This will make you more comfortable and powerful when riding and will help you avoid developing pain. You can be professionally fitted (expensive) or you can perform a rough basic bike fit by yourself (free).

***note:** Some people think it's better to have a dirty bike because they figure if it looks crappy, it's less likely to be stolen. If you try this strategy, make sure to at least clean the important parts of you bike like the brake pads, braking surfaces, chain pins, cables, and gears.
tip one: buy proper parts don't just make do with what you can find laying around.

Carry tweezers and a needle. If you get a flat tire, remove the tube and gently run your fingers along the inside of the tire to feel for any small objects like thorns or slivers of metal or tiny flecks of glass poking through. Tweezers and a needle make the removal of such small objects from the tire a lot easier. Removal is necessary or else the next tube you put in the tire will be punctured by the exact same object. Check the outer surface of the tire for other small objects partially embedded in it. Take them out to prevent them from embedding themselves farther in and causing another puncture while you ride. FYI, tires with features such as Kevlar and other protective linings are still susceptible to punctures, so don't make the mistake of thinking they are invulnerable.
